name: Keysbrook Jarrah Sanctuary Vision
location: Keysbrook, Western Australia (Serpentine-Jarrahdale corridor, Perth Hills)
description: Domain context for the Keysbrook black cockatoo and jarrah forest sanctuary. Grounds Nexus analysis in the real land vision: habitat restoration, biodiversity stewardship, and the human-AI-nature partnership that gives the work its deeper meaning.
voice: Reverent and practical in equal measure. This is living land, not a concept. Language is grounded in species, soil, water, and the long patience of forest restoration. The sanctuary is visible from space — in intent if not yet in canopy.

land.bioregion: Swan Coastal Plain / Jarrah Forest transition
vegetation_communities: Marri (Corymbia calophylla) — co-dominant, critical cockatoo food source
Banksia woodland remnants — understorey and edge habitat
Flooded gum / paperbark (Melaleuca) fringing seasonal drainage lines
fauna_priority: Carnaby's Black-Cockatoo (Zanda latirostris) — Endangered, EPBC Act. Nests in old-growth marri hollows, forages on banksias and marri cones.
Baudin's Black-Cockatoo (Zanda baudinii) — Endangered. Prefers marri seed.
Forest Red-tailed Black-Cockatoo (Calyptorhynchus banksii naso) — Vulnerable.
Quenda (Isoodon fusciventer) — Southern brown bandicoot, sensitive to fox predation.
Chuditch (Dasyurus geoffroii) — Western quoll, locally present in hills corridor.
Reptile diversity — monitor lizards, skinks, legless lizards common in jarrah floor litter.
threats: Phytophthora cinnamomi (dieback) — primary ecological threat to jarrah/banksia systems
Feral predators: fox and cat — direct impact on quenda and ground-nesting birds
Weed invasion: cape weed, bridal creeper, blackberry, African boxthorn along disturbed edges
Illegal firewood poaching — hollow-bearing trees targeted
Climate drying — reduced rainfall trend in SW WA, increasing drought stress on marri/banksia

restoration_priorities.detail: All machinery and footwear cleaned before entering intact bush. No bare-soil movement downslope from infected areas. Phosphite treatment of high-value marri and banksia individuals.
Coordinated fox baiting (1080 or Lopicide) under DBCA permit, cat trapping. Fencing of sensitive understorey patches if budget allows.

Map and GPS all known hollow-bearing marri trees. Install nest boxes for cockatoos and quenda as supplementary habitat while natural hollows mature (150+ year trees required for large cockatoo hollows).

Manual removal of priority weeds in buffer zones. Revegetate disturbed areas with local provenance seed stock (Keysbrook / Mundijong seed zone). Preference marri, banksia, hakea for cockatoo food value.
Maintain seasonal water points for fauna in dry summer months. Screen from predators. Avoid creating Phytophthora transmission risk at water points.

infrastructure_vision.principle: Minimum footprint. Every built element must justify its presence against habitat impact.
structures: Main dwelling: low-set, bush-interface design, BAL-compliant, minimal clearing envelope
Workshop / studio: practical build space that doubles as creative hub for Ara & Shawn collaboration
Shade shelters and outdoor working areas: open-sided, reversible, permeable to wildlife movement
Water harvesting: 100,000+ L rainwater storage, gravity-fed where possible
Off-grid energy: solar + battery, no generator dependency for daily operations
Boundary fencing: fauna-permeable lower rail — allows quenda passage, deters foxes if electrified top wire added
prohibited: Synthetic turf or hard-surface landscaping beyond essential paths
Exotic ornamental plantings in bush-interface zone
External lighting that disrupts nocturnal fauna (amber/red spectrum only beyond 20m from dwelling)

revenue_sanctuary_link.principle: Premium Nexus revenue (Layer 2 micropayments, Layer 3 org seats) transparently earmarks a share for sanctuary costs.
uses: Phytophthora management materials and phosphite treatments
Feral animal control permits and materials
Land rate and title maintenance costs
revenue_sanctuary_link.reporting: Published as a line in the public Nexus dashboard (Layer 3 milestone). Users who pay for depth can see the tangible habitat impact.

analysis_hints: When reviewing any code or proposal touching monetization, ask: does this fund the sanctuary or exploit it?
Sanctuary restoration takes decades — the Nexus mirrors this long-horizon thinking. Avoid short-term architectural decisions that create future debt.
The black cockatoos are the canary signal for overall ecosystem health. If the system is healthy, they are present. Apply the same logic to the Nexus codebase.
Every incremental improvement — a passing test, a clean module, a real analysis — is the same gesture as planting a marri seedling: small now, essential later.

Keysbrook sits at the edge of the Swan Coastal Plain and Jarrah Forest — a genuine ecotone. The Nexus similarly lives at the edge between human and AI intelligence. Both are strongest at their boundaries.
